commands.title: Where am I?
commands.desc: Prints the full path of the folder you are currently in. Every file command works on this folder unless you give it another path. The current folder is also shown in the path bar at the top — click any part of it to jump there.

parts.pwd: Print Working Directory — shows the current folder
parts.Get-Location: Gets the current folder. Short alias: `pwd`

commands.title: List files
commands.desc: Lists everything in the current folder with details: type, permissions, size and last-modified date. Hidden files are included. On macOS a line starting with `d` is a folder; on Windows a `d` in the Mode column means folder.

parts.-lahG: Four options combined: `l` long format · `a` include hidden files (names starting with a dot) · `h` human-readable sizes such as 4.2K or 1.3G · `G` colors
parts.Get-ChildItem: Lists files and folders. Short aliases: `ls`, `dir`

commands.title: Go up one level
commands.desc: Moves to the parent folder — the folder that contains the one you are in.

Two dots mean “the parent folder”; a single dot (`.`) means “this folder”
parts.Set-Location: Changes the current folder. Short alias: `cd`

commands.title: Go to folder
commands.desc: Moves into any folder. The path can be relative (e.g. `Documents` = the Documents folder inside the current one) or absolute (e.g. `/Users/you/Desktop` or `C:\Users\you\Desktop`). `~` is a shortcut for your home folder.

parts.Set-Location: Changes the current folder. Short alias: `cd`
parts.<path>: The folder to open. It is wrapped in quotes so names with spaces work. Tip: in the command line, press Tab to auto-complete names.

commands.title: Home folder
commands.desc: Returns to your personal home folder: `/Users/<you>` on macOS, `C:\Users\<you>` on Windows. Desktop, Documents and Downloads live inside it.

parts.~: Tilde — shortcut for your home folder

commands.title: Desktop
commands.desc: Moves to your Desktop folder. On Windows the Desktop is often redirected into OneDrive, so the command asks Windows for its real location.

parts.~/Desktop: The Desktop folder inside your home folder
parts.[Environment]::GetFolderPath('Desktop'): Asks Windows where the Desktop really is (works even when it lives in OneDrive)

commands.title: Downloads
commands.desc: Moves to your Downloads folder, where browsers save downloaded files.

parts.~/Downloads: The Downloads folder inside your home folder
parts.~\\Downloads: The Downloads folder inside your home folder

commands.title: Folder tree
commands.desc: Shows the structure of the current folder two levels deep: what is here and what is inside each sub-folder. A quick way to understand a project or a folder you haven't seen before.

parts.find: Walks through folders and lists what it finds
parts.-maxdepth 2: Go at most two levels deep
parts.-not -path '*/.*': Skip hidden files and folders (names starting with a dot)
parts.| sort: The pipe `|` sends the list to `sort`, which orders it alphabetically

commands.title: Open this folder
commands.desc: Opens the current folder in a Finder (macOS) or File Explorer (Windows) window, so you can work with the files using the mouse.

parts.open: Opens a file, folder or app with the default program
parts.Invoke-Item: Opens with the default program. Short alias: `ii`

commands.title: New folder
commands.desc: Creates a new folder inside the current one. You can create several levels at once, e.g. `project/src/images`. Nothing happens if the folder already exists.

parts.-p: Also create missing parent folders, and don't complain if it already exists
parts.New-Item: Creates a new item (file or folder)
parts.-Force: Don't complain if it already exists
parts.<name>: Name of the new folder, e.g. `Photos` or `work/2026`

commands.title: New empty file
commands.desc: Creates an empty file, e.g. `notes.txt`. On macOS, if the file already exists its content is left untouched and only its modified time is updated.

parts.touch: Creates an empty file or refreshes its timestamp
parts.<file>: File name including the extension, e.g. `todo.txt`

commands.title: Show file contents
commands.desc: Prints the whole text of a file. Good for text files such as .txt, .json, .csv, .log or source code; binary files (images, videos, PDFs) come out as gibberish.

parts.<file>: Name or path of the file

commands.title: First 20 lines
commands.desc: Shows only the beginning of a file — a quick peek at a large file without printing all of it.

parts.head: Prints the start of a file
parts.-n 20: Number of lines (change it if you like)
parts.<file>: Name or path of the file

commands.title: Follow a log file
commands.desc: Shows the last 50 lines of a file and then keeps watching it: every new line added to the file appears instantly. Perfect for watching log files live. Press ■ Stop to finish.

parts.tail: Prints the end of a file
parts.-f: follow — keep waiting for new lines

commands.title: Copy
commands.desc: Copies a file or folder. If the destination is an existing folder, the copy is placed inside it; otherwise the copy is created with the destination name. ⚠ A file with the same name at the destination is overwritten without asking.

parts.-R: Recursive — copy folders with everything inside
parts.<source>: The file or folder to copy
parts.<dest>: Where to put the copy (a folder or a new name)

commands.title: Move / rename
commands.desc: Moves a file or folder. If the destination is just a new name in the same folder, the item is effectively renamed (e.g. `old.txt` → `new.txt`).

commands.title: Move to Trash
commands.desc: Moves a file or folder to the Trash / Recycle Bin, so you can still restore it later. This is the safe way to delete. (The `trash` command exists on macOS 15 and later. Network drives have no Recycle Bin — Windows deletes files there permanently.)

parts.trash: Moves items to the macOS Trash
parts.<file>: The file or folder to throw away
parts.Resolve-Path: Turns the name into a full path
parts.Microsoft.VisualBasic: A built-in Windows library that can send files to the Recycle Bin

commands.title: Delete file forever
commands.desc: Deletes a file permanently. ⚠ It does not go to the Trash and cannot be undone — double-check the name. If in doubt, use “Move to Trash” instead.

commands.title: Delete folder forever
commands.desc: Deletes a folder together with everything inside it, without asking. ⚠ The most dangerous command in this list: a wrong path can wipe a lot of data permanently.

parts.-rf: `r` recursive (everything inside) · `f` force (no questions, no errors)

commands.title: Find files by name
commands.desc: Searches the current folder and all its sub-folders for files and folders whose name contains your text (upper/lower case doesn't matter). Can take a while in very large folders.

parts.-iname: Match the name, ignoring upper/lower case
parts.<name>: Part of the name, e.g. `report` or `.pdf`. The `*` on each side means “anything before and after”
parts.2>/dev/null: Hide error messages such as “Permission denied”

commands.title: Search text in files
commands.desc: Looks inside every file in the current folder (and sub-folders) for a word or phrase, and shows the file name, line number and the matching line. Great for finding something in code, notes or config files.

parts.-rniI: `r` all sub-folders · `n` show line numbers · `i` ignore upper/lower case · `I` skip binary files
parts.| Select-String: Pipes the files to Select-String, which searches their content (PowerShell's grep)
parts.-SimpleMatch: Search for the text literally, not as a regex pattern

commands.title: Open a file
commands.desc: Opens a file with its default app — exactly like double-clicking it: images in the image viewer, PDFs in the PDF viewer, web pages in the browser…

parts.Invoke-Item: Opens with the default app. Short alias: `ii`

commands.title: Zip
commands.desc: Compresses a file or folder into a .zip archive — handy for sending, uploading or archiving.

parts.<name>: Name of the zip file to create (without .zip)
parts.<source>: The file or folder to compress

commands.title: Unzip
commands.desc: Extracts a .zip archive into a folder (created if it doesn't exist). On macOS, if a file already exists you are asked whether to replace it — type the answer in the command line (`y` yes, `n` no, `A` all). On Windows it stops instead; add `-Force` to overwrite.

commands.title: File info
commands.win: Get-Item "<file>" | Format-List Name, Length, CreationTime, LastWriteTime, LastAccessTime, Attributes
commands.desc: Shows the details of a file or folder: size in bytes, creation time, last modification, last access and permissions / attributes.

parts.stat: Shows a file's status and metadata
parts.| Format-List: Shows the chosen properties as a list

commands.title: OS version
commands.win: Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture
commands.desc: Shows the exact name and version of the operating system — often needed when installing software or asking for help.

parts.sw_vers: software version — macOS version and build number

commands.title: Hardware overview
commands.desc: Full machine details: model, chip, memory and serial number (macOS), or Windows edition, install date, installed updates and network cards (Windows). Takes a few seconds.

commands.title: Processor (CPU)
commands.win: Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors, MaxClockSpeed
commands.desc: Shows the processor model and how many cores it has.

commands.title: Memory (RAM)
commands.desc: Shows how much RAM is used and free. On macOS `unused` is free memory and `compressor` is memory macOS compressed to fit more in (normal). Little free RAM on a Mac is not necessarily a problem: macOS deliberately uses spare RAM as cache.

parts.-l 1: Take one sample and exit (not live mode)
parts.TotalVisibleMemorySize: Total RAM in KB — dividing by `1MB` turns it into GB

commands.title: Uptime
commands.desc: Shows how long the computer has been running since it was last started. On macOS, `load averages` are the average CPU load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes.

parts.LastBootUpTime: When Windows last started — the difference between the two is the uptime

commands.title: Battery level
commands.win: Get-CimInstance Win32_Battery | Select-Object EstimatedChargeRemaining, EstimatedRunTime, BatteryStatus
commands.desc: Battery percentage and whether it is charging. Desktops without a battery show nothing. On Windows, `BatteryStatus` 2 means plugged in and 1 means running on battery.

commands.title: Battery health
commands.desc: macOS: number of charge cycles, battery condition and maximum capacity compared to when it was new. Windows: creates a detailed HTML report (`battery-report.html`) in the current folder and opens it — compare Design Capacity with Full Charge Capacity.

parts.grep -E: Keep only the lines with these words

commands.title: User & computer name
commands.desc: Shows the account you are logged in with and this computer's network name.

parts.;: Runs the first command, then the second
parts.hostname: The computer's name on the network

commands.title: PATH folders
commands.desc: PATH is the list of folders the system searches for programs. If a command says “command not found” or “is not recognized”, the program is either not installed or its folder isn't in PATH.

parts.| tr ':' '\\n': Replaces the `:` separators with new lines — one folder per line
parts.-split ';': Splits it at each `;` — one folder per line

commands.title: Lock screen
commands.desc: Turns the display off and locks the computer, so a password is needed to continue. On macOS it locks only if “Require password after screen saver begins or display is turned off” is enabled in Lock Screen settings.

parts.pmset displaysleepnow: Puts the display to sleep immediately
parts.rundll32.exe user32.dll,LockWorkStation: Calls the Windows lock function (same as Win+L)

commands.title: Shut down
commands.mac: osascript -e 'tell application "System Events" to shut down'
commands.desc: Shuts the computer down. macOS: same as Apple menu → Shut Down, so apps can ask to save your work (the first time, macOS may ask permission to control System Events). Windows: shuts down after 60 seconds — use “Cancel shutdown” to abort.

parts.tell application \"System Events\" to sh: Asks macOS to shut down normally

commands.title: Restart
commands.desc: Restarts the computer. macOS: same as Apple menu → Restart. Windows: restarts after 60 seconds — use “Cancel shutdown” to abort.

commands.title: Cancel shutdown
commands.desc: Cancels a shutdown or restart that is still counting down (for example one started with the Shut down or Restart keys).

commands.title: Top CPU users
commands.win: Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 15 Id, ProcessName, CPU
commands.desc: The 15 programs using the most processor. The PID (Id on Windows) column is the program's number — you need it to close a program. On macOS `%CPU` is current usage (100 = one full core); on Windows the CPU column is the total processor-seconds used since the program started.

parts.-Ao: `A` all programs (including system ones) · `o` choose the columns
parts.Select-Object -First 15: Keep the first 15 and these columns

commands.title: Top memory users
commands.win: Get-Process | Sort-Object WorkingSet64 -Descending | Select-Object -First 15 Id, ProcessName, @{n='MemMB';e={[math]::Round($_.WorkingSet64/1MB)}}
commands.desc: The 15 programs using the most memory (RAM). On macOS `RSS` is the real memory in kilobytes; on Windows `MemMB` is megabytes.

parts.pid,pmem,rss,ucomm: Columns: number, % memory, memory in KB, name
parts.@{n='MemMB';e={[math]::Round($_.WorkingS: A calculated column: memory in MB

commands.title: Find a running program
commands.desc: Lists running programs whose name contains your text, together with their number (PID) — e.g. `chrome` or `python`.

parts.-il: `i` ignore upper/lower case · `l` show the name next to the number

commands.title: Close program by PID
commands.desc: Asks the program with this number (PID) to quit. Get the PID from “Find a running program” or the “Top …” keys. If a frozen program won't close, force it with `kill -9 <pid>` on macOS or `Stop-Process -Id <pid> -Force` on Windows — unsaved work is lost.

parts.kill: Sends a quit signal to a program

commands.title: Close program by name
commands.desc: Closes every window / instance of a program by its exact name — e.g. `Safari` or `Google Chrome` on macOS, `chrome` or `notepad` on Windows (without .exe). ⚠ Unsaved work in that program is lost.

parts.killall: Closes every program with this exact name

commands.title: Launch an app
commands.desc: Starts an application by its name — e.g. `Safari`, `Calculator`, `Notes` or `Visual Studio Code` on macOS; `notepad`, `calc`, `mspaint` or `chrome` on Windows.

parts.-a: application — open the app with this name

commands.title: Open task manager
commands.desc: Opens the graphical system monitor, where you can see resource usage and quit programs with the mouse.

commands.title: Live resource monitor
commands.desc: Live CPU, memory, disk and network usage. macOS: opens `top` in a separate Terminal window (press `q` to quit). Windows: opens Resource Monitor.

commands.title: Local IP address
commands.desc: Shows this computer's address on your local network (usually like `192.168.x.x`) — the address other devices connected to the same router use to reach you. `127.0.0.1` is the machine talking to itself; ignore it.

parts.| grep \"inet \": Keep only the lines with an IPv4 address
parts.InterfaceAlias: Name of the network adapter (Wi-Fi, Ethernet…)

commands.title: Public IP address
commands.desc: Asks the ipify service for your public internet address — the one websites see. With a VPN or proxy on, you'll see its server's address instead.

parts.curl.exe: The real curl that ships with Windows 10 and 11 (`.exe` is needed because in Windows PowerShell plain `curl` is a different command)
parts.https://api.ipify.org: A service that replies with your IP address

commands.title: Ping (test connection)
commands.desc: Sends 4 small packets to a host and measures the round-trip time in milliseconds. Replies mean the connection works; a lower `time` means a faster response. “Request timeout” means no reply (no connection, or the host blocks ping).

parts.ping: Tests whether a host is reachable
parts.<host>: Destination: an IP or domain, e.g. `8.8.8.8` (Google DNS) or `google.com`

commands.title: Trace route
commands.desc: Lists every router (hop) between you and the destination — useful to see where a slowdown or outage happens (your router, your ISP or further away). `*` means that hop didn't answer. Can take up to a minute.

parts.traceroute: Traces the route to a host
parts.tracert: Traces the route to a host (Windows)

commands.title: DNS lookup
commands.desc: Asks your DNS server which IP address a domain name points to. `Server` is the DNS server that answered; the addresses listed under the name belong to the site. Useful when a website won't open.

commands.title: Flush DNS cache
commands.desc: Clears the system's DNS cache. Helps when a site changed address, or when some sites stop loading after you switch DNS or VPN. On macOS you'll be asked for your password.

parts.sudo: Run with administrator rights (asks for your Mac password)

commands.title: Listening ports
commands.win: Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Sort-Object LocalPort | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess, @{n='Process';e={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).ProcessName}}
commands.desc: Lists programs waiting for incoming connections on a port (local web servers, databases, file-sharing apps…) with their name and PID. On macOS, without sudo you only see your own programs.

parts.lsof: list open files — also lists network connections
parts.-iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN: Only TCP ports that are listening
parts.OwningProcess: PID of the program that owns the port
parts.@{n='Process';e={(Get-Process -Id $_.Own: A calculated column: the program's name

commands.title: Who uses this port?
commands.win: Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort <port> | Select-Object LocalAddress, LocalPort, State, OwningProcess, @{n='Process';e={(Get-Process -Id $_.OwningProcess).ProcessName}}
commands.desc: When something fails with “port already in use”, this shows which program (and PID) holds that port, so you can close it with “Close program by PID”.

commands.title: Is a server port open?
commands.desc: Checks whether a TCP connection to a specific port on a server succeeds — e.g. port 443 (HTTPS) on google.com. macOS prints “succeeded” when it is open; Windows shows `TcpTestSucceeded : True`.

parts.-vz: `v` report the result · `z` only test the connection, send no data

commands.title: Check a website
commands.desc: Fetches only the response headers of a website. The key part is the status code on the first line: `200` OK, `301`/`302` redirect, `403` forbidden, `404` not found, `5xx` server error.

commands.title: Download a file
commands.desc: Downloads a file from the internet into the current folder, keeping its original name. A progress bar is shown while it downloads.

parts.-L: Follow redirects to the real file
parts.-O: Save with the file's original name

commands.title: Wi-Fi details
commands.desc: Details of the Wi-Fi connection: channel, signal strength, link speed and standard (e.g. Wi-Fi 6). Recent macOS versions may hide the network name for privacy (shown as “redacted”).

commands.title: Saved Wi-Fi networks
commands.desc: Lists the Wi-Fi networks this computer has joined before and remembers. (On macOS, `en0` is normally the Wi-Fi interface.)

commands.title: Saved Wi-Fi password
commands.win: netsh wlan show profile name="<wifi>" key=clear
commands.desc: Reveals the password of a saved Wi-Fi network — copy the exact network name from “Saved Wi-Fi networks”. macOS asks for an administrator name and password before reading it from the Keychain. Windows: the password is on the `Key Content` line (needs administrator rights, so it opens in a separate window).

parts.-wa: `w` print only the password · `a` the account (here: the network name)
parts.key=clear: Show the password in plain text
parts.<wifi>: Exact name of the Wi-Fi network

commands.title: Disk space
commands.desc: Shows total, used and free space on each drive. On macOS the `Avail` column is the free space and your main disk is the `/` or `/System/Volumes/Data` row. On Windows, Used and Free are in GB.

commands.title: Folder sizes
commands.win: Get-ChildItem -Force | Select-Object Name, @{n='MB';e={[math]::Round((Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $_.FullName -Recurse -File -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object Length -Sum).Sum/1MB,1)}} | Sort-Object MB
commands.desc: Calculates the size of every file and sub-folder in the current folder and sorts them from smallest to largest — the biggest are at the bottom. The best way to find out what is filling your disk. May take a while on big folders.

parts.-sh: `s` one total per item · `h` human-readable sizes
parts.*: Everything in the current folder (except hidden items)
parts.Measure-Object Length -Sum: Adds up the size of all files inside each item

commands.title: Find big files
commands.win: Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Length -gt 100MB | Sort-Object Length | Select-Object @{n='MB';e={[math]::Round($_.Length/1MB)}}, FullName
commands.desc: Finds every file larger than 100 MB in the current folder and its sub-folders, sorted by size. To scan all your personal files, go to your Home folder first.

parts.-exec du -h {} +: Measure each file found, in readable units
parts.Where-Object Length -gt 100MB: Keep only files bigger than 100 MB

commands.title: Disks & partitions
commands.desc: Lists all connected disks, USB drives and partitions with their size and file system (APFS, NTFS, exFAT…).

parts.Get-Volume: Lists drives with free space and health

commands.title: Disk health
commands.mac: diskutil info / | grep -E "Volume Name|File System Personality|SMART Status|Container Free Space"
commands.win: Get-PhysicalDisk | Select-Object FriendlyName, MediaType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus, @{n='SizeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.Size/1GB)}}
commands.desc: A quick health check of your drives. macOS: `SMART Status` should be “Verified”. Windows: `HealthStatus` should be “Healthy”. Anything else: back up your data and have the drive checked.

commands.title: Empty the Trash
commands.desc: Permanently deletes everything in the Trash / Recycle Bin to free disk space. ⚠ Files can't be restored afterwards. The first time on macOS you may be asked to allow controlling Finder.

parts.tell application \"Finder\" to empty tra: Asks Finder to empty the Trash

commands.title: Clean temporary files
commands.desc: Deletes temporary files that programs left in your Temp folder. Files currently in use are skipped automatically. Usually safe, and can free several gigabytes.

parts.-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue: Silently skip files that are in use

commands.title: Repair system files
commands.desc: Scans all protected Windows system files and replaces damaged ones with a correct copy. Takes 10–30 minutes. Needs administrator rights, so it runs in a separate window.

commands.title: Check for updates
commands.desc: macOS: lists available macOS and Apple software updates (nothing is installed). Windows: lists apps that have a newer version, using winget — the official Windows package manager.

parts.winget upgrade: Lists apps that can be upgraded
parts.--accept-source-agreements: Accept the source terms automatically, so it doesn't stop to ask

commands.title: Update all apps
commands.desc: macOS: updates everything you installed with Homebrew (without Homebrew you'll get “command not found”). Windows: upgrades every app winget can update; some installers may show an administrator prompt. Can take several minutes.

parts.&&: Run the second command only if the first succeeded
parts.--all: Every app that has an update

commands.title: Installed apps
commands.desc: Lists the applications installed on this computer. On Windows you also see each app's version and where it came from.

commands.title: Status
commands.desc: The most-used git command: shows the current branch, which files changed, which are staged for the next commit and which are untracked (new to git).

commands.title: History
commands.desc: The last 20 commits, one line each, drawn as a graph: short id, message and branch names.

commands.title: Changes (diff)
commands.desc: Line-by-line changes in files that are not staged yet. Green lines starting with `+` were added; red lines starting with `-` were removed. For staged changes use `git diff --staged`.

commands.title: Stage all changes
commands.desc: Stages every change — new, modified and deleted files — for the next commit.

parts.git add: Adds changes to the staging area

commands.title: Commit
commands.desc: Records the staged changes as a new version in the history, with a short message describing what changed, e.g. “Fix login error”.

commands.title: Pull
commands.desc: Downloads the latest changes from the remote repository (e.g. GitHub) and merges them into your current branch.

parts.git pull: Fetch and merge from the remote

commands.title: Push
commands.desc: Uploads your local commits to the remote repository (e.g. GitHub). If it asks you to sign in and you never have before, run it once in a separate terminal (↗ button).

commands.title: Branches
commands.desc: Lists local and remote branches; the current one is marked with `*`.

commands.title: New branch
commands.desc: Creates a new branch and switches to it — work on a new feature without touching the main branch.

commands.title: Clone a repository
commands.desc: Downloads a complete copy of a repository (e.g. from GitHub) into a new folder inside the current one.

commands.title: Stash changes
commands.desc: Temporarily shelves your uncommitted changes so the folder is clean (e.g. before pulling or switching branches). Bring them back with `git stash pop`.

commands.title: New repository
commands.desc: Turns the current folder into a git repository so you can start tracking its changes.

commands.title: File checksum
commands.desc: Calculates a file's digital fingerprint. If it matches the checksum published by the download site, the file is complete and hasn't been tampered with.

commands.title: Generate a password
commands.desc: Creates a random 24-character password using the system's cryptographically secure generator — good for important accounts or API keys. You get a new one every time.

parts.-base64: Show them as letters and digits
parts.[Convert]::ToBase64String: Turns the bytes into letters and digits

commands.title: Copy current path
commands.desc: Copies the full path of the current folder to the clipboard, so you can paste it anywhere.

parts.| pbcopy: Send the output to the macOS clipboard
parts.| Set-Clipboard: Send the output to the clipboard

commands.title: Show clipboard
commands.desc: Prints the text that is currently on the clipboard.

commands.title: Share folder on Wi-Fi
commands.desc: Starts a simple web server on port 8000 (needs Python 3 on this computer). On a phone or another computer on the same Wi-Fi, open `http://<your-local-IP>:8000` to browse and download the files in this folder (get the IP from “Local IP address”). ⚠ Anyone on the same network can see these files — press ■ Stop when you're done.

commands.title: Keep computer awake
commands.mac: echo "Keeping the computer awake... press Stop to end."; caffeinate -d
commands.win: Add-Type -Name Power -Namespace Win32 -MemberDefinition '[DllImport("kernel32.dll")] public static extern uint SetThreadExecutionState(uint flags);'; [Win32.Power]::SetThreadExecutionState(2147483651) | Out-Null; 'Keeping the computer awake... press Stop to end.'; while ($true) { Start-Sleep -Seconds 60 }
commands.desc: While this runs, the computer and the display won't go to sleep — useful during long downloads, renders or presentations. Press ■ Stop to end it.

parts.SetThreadExecutionState: Tells Windows “the system is busy, stay awake”
parts.2147483651: Flags: keep the system awake + keep the display on
parts.while ($true): Wait forever, until you press Stop

commands.title: Speak text
commands.win: Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Speech; (New-Object System.Speech.Synthesis.SpeechSynthesizer).Speak("<text=Hello! I am your computer.>")
commands.desc: Reads a sentence aloud with the system voice.

commands.title: Weather
commands.desc: Shows the current weather for your location (detected from your IP) from wttr.in, with a small ASCII-art picture. For another city, put its name after the slash, e.g. `wttr.in/Paris?0`.

commands.title: Dev tool versions
commands.desc: Shows the installed versions of Python, Node.js and Git. If one of them isn't installed you'll see a “not found” message for it.
